claim: Perceptual decisions are biased toward higher-value options when overall gains can be improved.
source: Perceptual decisions are biased toward higher-value options when overall gains can be improved.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the study context, supported by the experimental design and results presented.

claim: Anticipatory preparation of higher-value actions began earlier, conferring a 'starting point' advantage at stimulus onset.
source: Anticipatory preparation of higher-value actions began earlier, conferring a 'starting point' advantage at stimulus onset
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG beta-band measurements showing earlier onset of motor preparation for high-value alternatives, as shown in Figure 2A and statistical analysis (F(1,16) = 15.8, p = 0.001).

claim: The delayed preparation of lower-value actions was steeper, conferring a value-opposed buildup-rate bias.
source: but the delayed preparation of lower-value actions was steeper, conferring a value-opposed buildup-rate bias.
evidence: This is supported by beta-band slope measurements showing steeper buildup rates for low-value alternatives (F(1,16) = 14.7, p = 0.001) as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A transient deflection toward the higher-value action was evoked by stimulus detection.
source: This, in turn, was countered by a transient deflection toward the higher-value action evoked by stimulus detection.
evidence: This is supported by LRP measurements showing a deflection in the direction of the cued choice beginning approximately 100 ms after stimulus onset (F(1,16) = 20.3, p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A neurally-constrained process model featuring anticipatory urgency, biased detection, and accumulation of growing stimulus-discriminating evidence successfully captured both behavior and motor preparation dynamics.
source: A neurally-constrained process model featuring anticipatory urgency, biased detection, and accumulation of growing stimulus-discriminating evidence, successfully captured both behavior and motor preparation dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting results showing the BurstIE model provided the best fit to behavioral data (Table 2) and successfully recapitulated motor preparation dynamics (Figure 4).

claim: Perceptual decision making is generally well explained by a process whereby evidence is accumulated over time up to a bound that can trigger an action.
source: Perceptual decision making is generally well explained by a process whereby evidence is accumulated over time up to a bound that can trigger an action (Brown and Heathcote, 2008; Link and Heath, 1975; Ratcliff, 1978; Smith and Ratcliff, 2004; Usher and McClelland, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature on evidence accumulation models.

claim: Faster and more accurate responses are made to higher value or more probable stimuli through modulating the starting point or drift rate of the decision process.
source: This simple scheme, developed primarily through the study of perceptual decisions with low-to-moderate speed pressure, affords two ways to explain how faster and more accurate responses are made to higher value or more probable stimuli: through modulating the starting point or drift rate of the process (Blangero and Kelly, 2017; Feng et al., 2009; Leite and Ratcliff, 2011; Mulder et al., 2012; Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Simen et al., 2009; Summerfield and Koechlin, 2010; Urai et al., 2019; Voss et al., 2004; White and Poldrack, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on value biasing mechanisms in decision-making.

claim: Corresponding adjustments to starting point or drift rate have been reported in neurophysiological recordings from motor-related areas of the brain.
source: Corresponding adjustments have been reported in neurophysiological recordings from motor-related areas of the brain (de Lange et al., 2013; Hanks et al., 2011; Rorie et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: When stimulus onset is predictable, anticipatory activity in motor preparation regions can begin to forge a decision even before the stimulus appears.
source: First, when stimulus onset is predictable, anticipatory activity in motor preparation regions can begin to forge a decision even before the stimulus appears.
evidence: This is supported by the observed pre-stimulus beta-band activity in the current study and citations to prior work.

claim: Anticipatory motor preparation is often dynamic, proceeding on a trajectory aimed at eventually crossing an action-triggering threshold by itself even in the absence of sensory input.
source: While standard models do allow for anticipatory processing in the setting of the starting point from which the accumulator evolves after sensory encoding, neurophysiological data have revealed that anticipatory motor preparation is often dynamic, proceeding on a trajectory aimed at eventually crossing an action-triggering threshold by itself even in the absence of sensory input (Feuerriegel et al., 2021; Kelly et al., 2021; Stanford et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies and is consistent with the dynamic pre-stimulus beta buildup observed in the current study.

claim: For many suddenly onsetting stimuli, sensory evidence of their distinguishing features emerges some time after the initial sensory neural response signaling their onset.
source: Second, for many suddenly onsetting stimuli, sensory evidence of their distinguishing features emerges some time after the initial sensory neural response signaling their onset (Afacan-Seref et al., 2018; Smith and Ratcliff, 2009), meaning that detection precedes discrimination.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the temporal dynamics of sensory processing.

claim: For random dot motion stimuli, it takes approximately 400 ms for direction information to stabilize after the onset of sensory encoding.
source: In the case of the widely studied random dot motion stimulus, recent work shows that behavior is well captured by a model in which accumulation begins at the onset of sensory encoding but where it takes a further 400 ms approximately for the direction information to stabilize (Smith and Lilburn, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smith and Lilburn, 2020.

claim: Serial detection and discrimination phases are reflected in human electrophysiological signatures of differential motor preparation during fast, value-biased decisions.
source: In fact, serial detection and discrimination phases are reflected in human electrophysiological signatures of differential motor preparation during fast, value-biased decisions about other sensory features. Specifically, these signals show biased stimulus-evoked changes initially in the direction of higher value before being re-routed toward the correct sensory alternative (Afacan-Seref et al., 2018; Noorbaloochi et al., 2015), in line with previously proposed dual-phase models (Diederich and Busemeyer, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies and is consistent with the LRP findings in the current study.

claim: Accuracy was higher for high-value trials than low-value trials (F(1,16) = 60.8, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.79).
source: Repeated measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) with fixed effects for task condition and value demonstrated that accuracy was higher for high-value trials than low-value trials (F(1,16) = 60.8, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.79)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Median RTs for correct responses were shorter for high-value trials than low-value trials (F(1,16) = 80.7, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.84).
source: and the median RTs for correct responses were shorter (F(1,16) = 80.7, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.84).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Task condition affected accuracy (F(3,48) = 60.2, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.79).
source: In addition to the large value effects, task condition affected accuracy (F(3,48) = 60.2, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.79)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Task condition affected correct RTs (F(3,48) = 38.1, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.61).
source: and correct RTs (F(3,48) = 38.1, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.61)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The high-coherence conditions were more accurate than other conditions (p < 0.001 for blocked and interleaved).
source: the high-coherence conditions were more accurate (p < 0.001 for blocked and interleaved)
evidence: This claim is supported by pairwise comparisons of accuracy data.

claim: The blocked high-coherence condition was the fastest (p < 0.001 compared to other three conditions).
source: and the blocked high-coherence condition, with the shorter deadline, was the fastest (p < 0.001 compared to other three conditions).
evidence: This claim is supported by pairwise comparisons of RT data.

claim: Decreases in spectral amplitude in the beta band over motor cortex reliably occur with the preparation and execution of movement.
source: Decreases in spectral amplitude in the beta band (integrated over 14–30 Hz) over motor cortex reliably occur with the preparation and execution of movement (Pfurtscheller, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature on beta-band motor activity.

claim: The beta signal contralateral to each hand leading up to the response reflects effector-selective motor preparation that is predictive of choice.
source: When the alternative responses in a decision task correspond to movements of the left and right hands, the signal located contralateral to each hand leading up to the response appears to reflect effector-selective motor preparation that is predictive of choice (Donner et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on lateralized motor preparation signals.

claim: Before stimulus onset, the 'starting levels' of beta signals reflect biased motor preparation when prior expectations are biased.
source: Furthermore, before the onset of sensory evidence the 'starting levels' of the signals reflect biased motor preparation when prior expectations are biased (de Lange et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and is consistent with the pre-stimulus beta differences observed in the current study.

claim: Beta signals are higher under speed pressure for both alternatives.
source: and are higher under speed pressure for both alternatives (Kelly et al., 2021; Murphy et al., 2016; Steinemann et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The beta signal contralateral to the chosen hand reaches a highly similar level at response irrespective of stimulus conditions or RT.
source: The signal contralateral to the chosen hand then reaches a highly similar level at response irrespective of stimulus conditions or RT, consistent with a fixed, action-triggering threshold (Devine et al., 2019; Feuerriegel et al., 2021; Kelly et al., 2021; O'Connell et al., 2012; Steinemann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The level of beta before stimulus onset predicts RT.
source: The level of beta before stimulus onset also predicts RT, and its post-stimulus buildup-rate scales with evidence strength
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Steinemann et al., 2018).

claim: Beta post-stimulus buildup-rate scales with evidence strength.
source: The level of beta before stimulus onset also predicts RT, and its post-stimulus buildup-rate scales with evidence strength, underlining that this signal reflects both evidence-independent and evidence-dependent contributions to the decision process (Steinemann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Motor preparation for the high-value alternative was greater than that for the low-value alternative 750 ms after the cue (F(1,16) = 17.6, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.52).
source: Preparation for the high-value alternative was greater than that for the low-value alternative 750 ms after the cue (F(1,16) = 17.6, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.52).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of beta-band amplitude data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The buildup rates of motor preparation signals for the low-value alternative were significantly steeper (slope from 700 to 800 ms, F(1,16) = 14.7, p = 0.001, partial η2 = 0.48).
source: However, despite their later onset, the buildup rates of motor preparation signals for the low-value alternative were significantly steeper (slope from 700 to 800 ms, F(1,16) = 14.7, p = 0.001, partial η2 = 0.48), indicating a negative buildup-rate bias.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of beta-band slope data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority of individuals (14 out of 17) show steeper buildup for the low-value alternative.
source: Despite absolute levels of beta amplitude varying quite widely across the group, as is typical in human EEG, the majority of individuals (14 out of 17) show steeper buildup for the low-value alternative.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by individual participant data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The bias in relative motor preparation favoring the high-value cue peaked at around 600 ms post-cue and then began to decline before stimulus onset.
source: As a consequence of these differences in onset and buildup rate, the bias in relative motor preparation favoring the high-value cue peaked at around 600 ms post-cue and then began to decline before stimulus onset (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the relative beta amplitude timecourse shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Beginning approximately 100 ms after the stimulus, there was a deflection in the LRP in the direction of the cued choice (F(1,16) = 20.3, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.56).
source: Beginning approximately 100 ms after the stimulus, there was a deflection in the direction of the cued choice (in the correct direction for high-value trials and incorrect direction for low-value trials, F(1,16) = 20.3, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.56, effect of value on the mean LRP from 150 to 180 ms, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of LRP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The sensory evidence appears to begin to affect motor preparation at around 150 ms when the LRP for the low-value trials begins to turn around and build in the correct direction.
source: The sensory evidence appears to begin to affect motor preparation at around 150 ms when the LRP for the low-value trials begins to turn around and build in the correct direction.
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of the LRP timecourse shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The diffusion decision model (DDM) describes a one-dimensional stationary evidence-accumulation process beginning somewhere between two decision bounds and ending when one of the bounds is crossed.
source: Probably the most widely used evidence accumulation model for two alternative decision making is the diffusion decision model (DDM, Ratcliff, 1978), which describes a one-dimensional stationary evidence-accumulation process beginning somewhere between two decision bounds and ending when one of the bounds is crossed, triggering the associated response action.
evidence: This claim describes the DDM framework and is supported by a citation to Ratcliff, 1978.

claim: Value biases in the DDM framework are traditionally incorporated by either biasing the starting point closer to one bound or biasing the rate of evidence accumulation.
source: Traditionally, value biases can be incorporated into this framework by either biasing the starting point closer to one bound than the other or biasing the rate of evidence accumulation, the former of which generally better describes behavior (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008).
evidence: This claim describes traditional approaches to modeling value biases and is supported by a citation.

claim: When there is a need to respond quickly, a stationary evidence-accumulation model is not sufficient to capture the pattern of value biases in behavior.
source: However, researchers have found that when there is a need to respond quickly, a stationary evidence-accumulation model is not sufficient to capture the pattern of value biases in behavior, which exhibits a dynamic transition from early, value-driven responses to later evidence-based ones.
evidence: This claim is supported by the subsequent citations to models with nonstationary drift rates.

claim: Accounting for fast value-biased behavior in a DDM framework has required a nonstationary drift rate.
source: Accounting for this fast value-biased behavior in a DDM framework has instead required a nonstationary drift rate; either a dual-phase model with an initial value-based drift-rate transitioning to a later evidence-based one (Diederich and Busemeyer, 2006), or combining a constant drift-rate bias with a gradually increasing sensory evidence function (Afacan-Seref et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: The increasing-evidence (IE) models performed better than the stationary-evidence (SE) models.
source: The increasing-evidence (IE) models performed better than the stationary-evidence (SE) models, with the BurstIE model providing the best fit to behavior (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by model comparison results shown in Table 2.

claim: The BurstIE model provided the best fit to behavior.
source: The increasing-evidence (IE) models performed better than the stationary-evidence (SE) models, with the BurstIE model providing the best fit to behavior (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by model comparison results shown in Table 2, with the lowest AIC and highest Akaike weight.

claim: The BurstIE model captured all the main qualitative features of the RT distributions, including the indistinguishable leading edges of correct high-value and incorrect low-value trials.
source: This model captured all the main qualitative features of the RT distributions, including the indistinguishable (value-driven) leading edges of correct high-value and incorrect low-value trials (Figure 4D, E)
evidence: This claim is supported by visual comparison of model fits to data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The BurstIE model captured the transition from value- to evidence-based responses visible in the low-value conditional accuracy functions (CAFs).
source: and the transition from value- to evidence-based responses visible in the low-value conditional accuracy functions (CAFs, Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual comparison of model fits to CAF data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Allowing the urgency rates to be free parameters but unbiased by value did not capture the behavior as well as the constrained BurstIE model.
source: First, allowing the urgency rates to be free parameters, but unbiased by value (Kelly et al., 2021), did not capture the behavior as well as the constrained BurstIE model.
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison results shown in Table 2.

claim: A model with constrained urgency but no stimulus-evoked bias produced a far inferior fit.
source: Then, a model with constrained urgency but no stimulus-evoked bias produced a far inferior fit.
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison results shown in Table 2 (Urgency-only bias model).

claim: Swapping the neural constraints across regimes substantially worsened the fit.
source: We then verified the specific contribution of quantitative differences across regimes in the urgency effects measured in the beta signals by showing that swapping the neural constraints across regimes substantially worsened the fit.
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison results shown in Table 2 (Constraints-Swap models).

claim: The DDM performance was markedly worse than all of the neurally constrained alternatives.
source: To serve as a benchmark, we also fit the DDM, with stationary evidence accumulation and allowing for bias only in the starting point of evidence accumulation (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008), whose performance was markedly worse than all of the neurally constrained alternatives.
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison results shown in Table 2, where the DDM has a much higher AIC (634) compared to other models.

claim: The BurstIE model was strongly preferred for all jackknifed samples.
source: The BurstIE model was strongly preferred for all of the samples (see Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the jackknife analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Rather than simply enhancing all parameters of the decision process in favor of high-value alternatives, the neural decision architecture has the flexibility to apply biases in opposing directions to different process components.
source: Together, the findings show that, rather than simply enhancing all parameters of the decision process in favor of high-value alternatives, the neural decision architecture has the flexibility to apply biases in opposing directions to different process components, in a way that affords low-value decision signals the chance to 'catch up' when smaller rewards can be attained.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the overall pattern of results showing positive starting point bias but negative urgency-rate bias.

claim: Convergent evidence from motor preparation signals and behavioral modeling demonstrated that a dynamic sequence of opposing value biases and nonstationary evidence accumulation all played important roles in forming the rapid, multiphasic decisions on this task.
source: Convergent evidence from motor preparation signals and behavioral modeling demonstrated that a dynamic sequence of opposing value biases and nonstationary evidence accumulation all played important roles in forming the rapid, multiphasic decisions on this task.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined EEG and modeling results presented throughout the paper.

claim: The value bias was largely concentrated in the early part of the decision process.
source: In agreement with previous research that has called for nonstationary accounts of value biasing in time-pressured decisions (Diederich and Busemeyer, 2006), we found that the value bias was largely concentrated in the early part of the process.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model comparison favoring the BurstIE model with transient bias over sustained bias models, and by citation to prior work.

claim: The particular dynamics of the RDK stimulus, featuring a substantial lag between stimulus onset and the emergence of discriminatory sensory evidence, may have provided a focal point for the bias to be expressed separately from the evidence itself.
source: The particular dynamics of the RDK stimulus, featuring a substantial lag between stimulus onset and the emergence of discriminatory sensory evidence, may have provided a focal point for the bias to be expressed separately from the evidence itself; indeed the model comparison very clearly favored the growing sensory evidence and noise.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why the increasing evidence model performed better, based on the known properties of RDK stimuli.

claim: The signature expressions of sequential detection-discrimination effect are observed also for discriminations of stimulus displacement and color.
source: However, the signature expressions of this sequential detection–discrimination effect—namely, the almost purely value-driven nature of both the leading edge of RT distributions and of the initial stimulus-evoked LRP deflection—are observed also for discriminations of stimulus displacement (Noorbaloochi et al., 2015) and color (Afacan-Seref et al., 2018), suggesting the phenomenon generalizes beyond the RDK stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies showing similar effects with different stimulus types.

claim: The dynamic shift from value to evidence-driven accumulation is reminiscent of conflict tasks.
source: The dynamic shift from value to evidence-driven accumulation is reminiscent of conflict tasks, for which a stationary drift rate is similarly insufficient to describe the observed behavioral patterns.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between the current findings and conflict task literature, supported by subsequent discussion.

claim: In conflict tasks, the context in which a perceptual stimulus is presented can be congruent with either the correct or the incorrect response, with the latter causing conflict that results in slower and more error-prone responding.
source: In these tasks, the context in which a perceptual stimulus is presented (i.e., features of the stimulus that are irrelevant to the task requirements) can be congruent with either the correct or the incorrect response. The latter case causes conflict that results in slower and more error-prone responding (Eriksen and Eriksen, 1974; Lu and Proctor, 1995; MacLeod, 1991), and produces signatures of competing motor plans in the LRP that are similar to those found here (Gratton et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim describes conflict task phenomena and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Prominent accounts of conflict tasks posit that an automatic processing of the stimulus happens in parallel with the controlled (decision) process.
source: Prominent accounts of these tasks posit that an automatic processing of the stimulus happens in parallel with the controlled (decision) process (Servant et al., 2016; Ulrich et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim describes theoretical accounts of conflict tasks and is supported by citations.

claim: The anticipatory mu/beta buildup activity in conflict tasks is unbiased because the conflict does not arise until after stimulus onset.
source: Indeed, the patterns of biased anticipatory motor preparation we see in this study cannot be present in tasks where the conflict does not arise until after stimulus onset; in such tasks the anticipatory mu/beta buildup activity while present is unbiased (Feuerriegel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on conflict tasks.

claim: The fact that beta buildup happens earlier under speed pressure suggests that it is strategic rather than automatic.
source: In the case of these beta signals, the fact that the buildup happens earlier under speed pressure (Kelly et al., 2021) suggests that they are much more likely to be strategic rather than automatic
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior research showing speed pressure effects on beta signals.

claim: A negative drift-rate bias featured alongside a starting point bias in the optimal decision strategy under certain assumed bound settings in the context of the DDM with unequal prior probabilities.
source: In the context of the DDM with unequal prior probabilities, Moran, 2015 found that a negative drift-rate bias featured alongside a starting point bias in the optimal decision strategy under certain assumed bound settings, albeit not when bound settings were assumed controllable as part of the optimization calculation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moran, 2015.

claim: A tradeoff between the positive starting level bias and negative urgency-rate bias may have arisen from the fact that the greater the starting point bias, the greater the need for a steeper low-value urgency signal to give it a chance to overtake the high-value signal when the low-value DV represents the correct response.
source: Here, a similar tradeoff between the positive starting level bias and negative urgency-rate bias may have arisen from the fact that the greater the starting point bias, the greater the need for a steeper low-value urgency signal to give it a chance to overtake the high-value signal when the low-value DV represents the correct response.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed biasing pattern.

claim: Understanding the processes generating the behaviors in this task rested on the neurophysiological identification of strategic urgency biases.
source: Understanding the processes generating the behaviors in this task rested on the neurophysiological identification of strategic urgency biases.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the importance of the EEG constraints for the modeling work.

claim: The anticipatory nature of the early beta signal buildup aided in specifically linking it to evidence-independent urgency.
source: The anticipatory nature of the early beta signal buildup aided in specifically linking it to evidence-independent urgency, and its incorporation in the model was key to understanding the subsequent processing of the motion stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the value of the pre-stimulus beta measurements for model development.

claim: The finding of a negative urgency-rate bias as part of the participants' dominant strategy highlights the broad range of dynamic adjustments that can be made during fast-paced sensorimotor decisions.
source: Nevertheless, the finding of a negative urgency-rate bias as part of the participants' dominant strategy highlights the broad range of dynamic adjustments that can be made during fast-paced sensorimotor decisions.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the implications of the negative urgency-rate bias finding.

claim: Seventeen participants completed the two EEG sessions.
source: Eighteen participants (eight female) thus completed the two EEG sessions.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of participants, though note that one was later excluded, leaving 17 in the final analysis.

claim: Motor preparation biasing effects tend to be consistent and robust with effect sizes of at least d = 1 for similar 'bolus' effects.
source: Motor preparation biasing effects tend to be consistent and robust (e.g., effect sizes of at least d = 1 for similar 'bolus' effects in Afacan-Seref et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 15-18 participants provide 80% power to detect medium-to-large effect sizes.
source: and 15–18 participants provide 80% power to detect medium-to-large effect sizes.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical power based on standard power analysis principles.

claim: The RDK stimulus had a dot density of 16.7 dots per °/s.
source: The dot density was 16.7 dots per °/s.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus parameters.

claim: One-third of the total number of dots was visible on screen at any one time in the RDK stimulus.
source: One-third of the total number of dots was visible on screen at any one time; each dot remained on screen for one 13.3-ms frame and was replotted two frames later as the three sets of dots were alternated.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus parameters.

claim: The first onset of coherent motion occurred 40 ms (three frames) after the onset of the RDK stimulus.
source: The first onset of coherent motion thus occurred 40 ms (three frames) after the onset of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the temporal properties of the stimulus.

claim: RTs less than 50 ms (0.23% of trials) were excluded from analyses and model fitting.
source: RTs less than 50 ms (0.23% of trials) were excluded from analyses and model fitting.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: Trials without a response (0.21% of trials) were excluded.
source: Responses up to and beyond the deadline were included in all analyses so long as they occurred before the end of the RDK stimulus; trials without a response (0.21% of trials) were excluded.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: One participant was an outlier in terms of biasing and was excluded from further analyses.
source: One participant was an outlier in terms of biasing (error rate difference between low- and high-value trials fell more than two interquartile ranges above the upper quartile) and was excluded from further analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant exclusion.

claim: Continuous EEG data from 128 scalp electrodes were acquired using an ActiveTwo system and digitized at 1024 Hz.
source: Continuous EEG data from 128 scalp electrodes were acquired using an ActiveTwo system (BioSemi, The Netherlands) and digitized at 1024 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the EEG recording parameters.

claim: EEG data were low-pass filtered with a 3 dB corner frequency of 37 Hz.
source: EEG data were low-pass filtered by convolution with a 137-tap Hanning-windowed sinc function designed to provide a 3 dB corner frequency of 37 Hz with strong attenuation at the mains frequency (50 Hz), and detrended.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the signal processing methods.

claim: Current source density transformation was applied to the single-trial epochs to mitigate the effects of volume conduction across the scalp.
source: Then, to mitigate the effects of volume conduction across the scalp, current source density transformation was applied to the single-trial epochs (Kayser and Tenke, 2006; Kelly and O'Connell, 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the signal processing methods, supported by citations.

claim: Beta-band activity was measured as the mean amplitude in the range 14-30 Hz.
source: Beta-band activity was measured using a short-time Fourier transform applied to 300-ms windows stepped by 25 ms at a time, and by taking the mean amplitude in the range 14–30 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the signal processing methods.

claim: Beta was measured from electrodes selected per individual based on exhibiting the strongest decrease at response relative to cue or stimulus onset.
source: To ensure precise measurements for model constraints, beta was measured from electrodes selected per individual based on exhibiting the strongest decrease at response relative to cue or stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electrode selection procedure.

claim: Standard sites C3/C4 were selected by default where difference topography foci were close and symmetric (9 of 17 participants).
source: Standard sites C3/C4 were selected by default where difference topography foci were close and symmetric (9 of 17 participants)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electrode selection procedure.

claim: For individually selected electrodes, the contralateral beta just prior to response (-50 ms) reached a threshold across conditions.
source: For these individually selected electrodes (marked in Figure 5A), the contralateral beta just prior to response (−50 ms) reached a threshold across conditions (Figure 5B; the error bars in Figure 2B break this down further into value and response conditions).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ipsilateral beta diverged between the blocked high coherence and the other conditions, indicating a closer race for the most speed-pressured condition.
source: The ipsilateral beta diverged between the blocked high coherence and the other conditions, indicating a closer race for the most speed-pressured condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ipsilateral beta patterns shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When standard C3/C4 sites were selected, there was an offset between the blocked conditions and the interleaved conditions.
source: When the standard C3/C4 sites were instead selected, however, we found an offset between the blocked conditions and the interleaved conditions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The blocked and interleaved sessions were performed on different days for all participants.
source: This was unexpected, but not entirely surprising due to the fact that the blocked and interleaved sessions were performed on different days for all participants
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Models were fit to the group average of the RT quantiles.
source: Models were fit to the group average of the RT quantiles (see Methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the modeling approach.

claim: Grand-average beta-amplitude dynamics are much more robust than those of individuals.
source: We did not fit the models to individual participants because, in contrast to models solely fit to behavior where each individual's data can be taken as an accurate reflection of the outcomes of their true individual decision process, our neurally constrained models constrain certain key parameters to equal EEG beta-amplitude measures. These EEG measures are much less reliable on an individual-participant level, where it is not unusual to have certain individuals showing no signal at all due to factors independent of the decision process such as brain geometry. We therefore conduct the modeling on a grand-average level because grand-average beta-amplitude dynamics are much more robust.
evidence: This is a justification for the modeling approach based on the properties of EEG signals.
